title: Philosophers who saw God and worshipped idols
source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ οἱ τοιαῦτα περὶ τοῦ πρώτου ἀγαθοῦ γράψαντες καταβαίνουσιν „εἰς Πειραιέα,“ προσευξόμενοι ὡς θεῷ τῇ Ἀρτέμιδι καὶ ὀψόμενοι τὴν ὑπὸ ἰδιωτῶν ἐπιτελουμένην πανήγυριν· καὶ τηλικαῦτά γε φιλοσοφήσαντες περὶ τῆς ψυχῆς καὶ τὴν διαγωγὴν τῆς καλῶς βεβιωκυΐας διεξελθόντες, καταλιπόντες τὸ μέγεθος ὧν „αὐτοῖς“ „ὁ θεὸς“ „ἐφανέρωσεν“ εὐτελῆ φρονοῦσι καὶ μικρὰ, „ἀλεκτρυόνα“ „τῷ Ἀσκληπιῷ“ ἀποδιδόντες· καὶ „τὰ“ „ἀόρατα“ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τὰς ἰδέας φαντασθέντες „ἀπὸ τῆς κτίσεως τοῦ κόσμου“ καὶ τῶν αἰσθητῶν, ἀφ᾿ ὧν ἀναβαίνουσιν ἐπὶ τὰ νοούμενα, τήν τε ἀΐδιον αὐτοῦ δύναμιν καὶ θειότητα οὐκ ἀγεννῶς ἰδόντες οὐδὲν ἧττον „ἐματαιώθησαν ἐν τοῖς διαλογισμοῖς αὐτῶν,“ καὶ ὡς „ἀσύνετος αὐτῶν (ἡ) καρδία“ ἐν σκότῳ καὶ ἀγνοίᾳ καλινδεῖται τῇ περὶ τοῦ θεραπεύειν τὸ θεῖον. καὶ ἔστιν ἰδεῖν τοὺς ἐπὶ σοφίᾳ μέγα φρονοῦντας καὶ θεολογίᾳ „ὁμοιώματι εἰκόνος φθαρτοῦ ἀνθρώπου“ προσκυνοῦντας, εἰς τιμήν φησιν ἐκείνου, ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε δὲ καὶ καταβαίνοντας μετ᾿ Αἰγυπτίων ἐπὶ τὰ πετεινὰ ἢ τετράποδα ἢ ἑρπετά. ἵνα δὲ καὶ δοκῶσί τινες ταῦτα ὑπεραναβεβηκέναι, ἀλλ᾿ εὑρεθήσονται ἀλλάξαντες „τὴν ἀλήθειαν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν τῷ ψεύδει“ καὶ σέβοντες καὶ λατρεύοντες „τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα.“ διόπερ τῶν ἐν Ἕλλησι σοφῶν καὶ πολυμαθῶν τοῖς ἔργοις περὶ τὸ θεῖον πλανωμένων „ἐξελέξατο ὁ θεὸς“ „τὰ μωρὰ τοῦ κόσμου,“ „ἵνα καταισχύνῃ τοὺς σοφοὺς,“ „καὶ τὰ ἀγενῆ“ „καὶ τὰ ἀσθενῆ“ „καὶ τὰ ἐξουθενημένα“ καὶ „τὰ μὴ ὄντα, ἵνα τὰ ὄντα καταργήσῃ“· καὶ ἀληθῶς, ἵνα „μὴ καυχήσηται πᾶσα σὰρξ ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ.“ πρῶτον δὲ ἡμῶν σοφοὶ, Μωϋσῆς ὁ ἀρχαιότατος καὶ οἱ ἑξῆς αὐτῷ προφῆται, „οὐδαμῶς“ „ῥητὸν“ ἐπιστάμενοι τὸ πρῶτον ἀγαθὸν ἔγραψαν μὲν, ὡς θεοῦ (ἑαυτὸν) ἐμφανίζοντος τοῖς ἀξίοις καὶ ἐπιτηδείοις, ὅτι „ὤφθη“ ὁ θεὸς (φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν) τῷ Ἀβραὰμ ἢ τῷ Ἰσαὰκ ἢ τῷ Ἰακώβ. τίς δὲ ὢν ὤφθη καὶ ποταπὸς καὶ τίνα τρόπον καὶ τίνι τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν, καταλελοίπασιν ἐξετάζειν τοῖς δυναμένοις ἑαυτοὺς ἐμπαρέχειν παραπλησίους ἐκείνοις, οἷς ὤφθη ὁ θεός· ὀφθεὶς αὐτῶν οὐ τοῖς τοῦ σώματος ὀφθαλμοῖς ἀλλὰ τῇ καθαρᾷ καρδίᾳ. καὶ γὰρ κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἡμῶν „μακάριοι οἱ καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ, ὅτι αὐτοὶ τὸν θεὸν ὄψονται.“
pass_a_gloss: But those who wrote such things about the first good go down (καταβαίνω) 'to the Piraeus', to pray (προσεύχομαι) to Artemis as to a god and to see the festival (πανήγυρις) carried out (ἐπιτελέω) by ordinary people (ἰδιῶται); and having philosophized (φιλοσοφέω) such great things about the soul and gone through (διεξέρχομαι) the way of life (διαγωγή) of the soul that has lived well, leaving the greatness of the things which 'God showed them', they think (φρονέω) cheap (εὐτελής) and small things, rendering (ἀποδίδωμι) 'a cock (ἀλεκτρυών) to Asclepius'; and having imagined (φαντάζομαι) 'the invisible things' of God and the ideas (ἰδέαι) 'from the creation of the world' and from the sensible things (αἰσθητά), from which they ascend (ἀναβαίνω) to the intelligible things (νοούμενα), and having seen not ignobly (ἀγεννῶς) his everlasting power and divinity, no less 'were made vain in their reasonings', and as 'their unintelligent heart' rolls about (καλινδέομαι) in darkness (σκότος) and ignorance (ἄγνοια) concerning the serving (θεραπεύω) of the divine (τὸ θεῖον). And one can see those thinking big (μέγα φρονέω) about wisdom and theology (θεολογία) bowing down (προσκυνέω) to 'a likeness of an image of corruptible man', for honour, he/they say, of that one (ἐκεῖνος), and sometimes going down with Egyptians to the birds or quadrupeds or reptiles. And even if some seem to have gone up beyond (ὑπεραναβαίνω) these, they will be found having exchanged 'the truth of God in the lie (ψεῦδος)' and revering (σέβω) and serving (λατρεύω) 'the creation (κτίσις) beyond (παρά) the one who created (κτίζω)'. Therefore, the wise and much-learned (πολυμαθεῖς) among Greeks wandering (πλανάομαι) in deeds (ἔργα) about the divine, 'God chose (ἐκλέγομαι) the foolish things of the world, that he might shame (καταισχύνω) the wise, and the low-born (ἀγενῆ) and the weak (ἀσθενῆ) and the despised (ἐξουθενημένα)' and 'the things that are not, that he might abolish (καταργέω) the things that are'; and truly, that 'all flesh may not boast (καυχάομαι) before God.' First (πρῶτον) our wise men, Moses the most ancient and the prophets after him, knowing the first good 'in no way' 'sayable', wrote indeed, as God manifesting (ἐμφανίζω) (himself) to the worthy (ἄξιοι) and suitable (ἐπιτήδειοι), that God 'appeared (ὤφθη)', say, to Abraham or Isaac or Jacob. But who being he appeared, and of what sort (ποταπός), and in what manner (τρόπος), and to which of the things in us, they have left to examine to those able to present (ἐμπαρέχω) themselves similar to those to whom God appeared; having been seen (ὀφθείς) by them not with the eyes of the body but with the pure (καθαρός) heart. For according to our Jesus: 'blessed (μακάριοι) the pure in heart, for they shall see God.'
pass_b_english: Yet those who wrote such things about the first good go down “to the Piraeus” to pray to Artemis as a goddess and to watch the festival held by the common people (Plato, Republic 1.327a). After philosophizing so loftily about the soul and describing the life of the soul that has lived well, they abandon the greatness of what “God showed them” (Romans 1:19) and think mean and petty thoughts, paying “a cock to Asclepius” (Plato, Phaedo 118a). And though they pictured to themselves “the invisible things” of God and the ideas “from the creation of the world” and from the things of sense, from which they ascend to the things known by the mind, and though they saw, not ignobly, his eternal power and divinity, they nonetheless “became futile in their reasonings” (Romans 1:20–21), and their “senseless heart” (Romans 1:21), as it were, wallows in darkness and ignorance about the worship of the divine.

And one can see men who pride themselves on their wisdom and their theology bowing down to “the likeness of an image of corruptible man” (Romans 1:23), in honour, so it is said, of that being, and sometimes even going down with the Egyptians to birds or four-footed beasts or creeping things. And even if some seem to have risen above these things, they will still be found to have “exchanged the truth of God for a lie” and to be worshipping and serving “the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25).

Therefore, since the wise and learned among the Greeks go astray in their deeds concerning the divine, “God chose” “the foolish things of the world” “to put the wise to shame”, “and the base things” “and the weak things” “and the things despised”, and “the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are” (1 Corinthians 1:27–28); and truly, so that “no flesh may boast before God” (1 Corinthians 1:29).

But our own wise men, Moses, the most ancient of all, and the prophets after him, were the first to know that the first good can “by no means” be “spoken”. They did write, since God shows himself to those who are worthy and fit, that God “appeared”, for example, to Abraham or to Isaac or to Jacob (Genesis 12:7; Genesis 26:24; Genesis 35:9; Exodus 6:3). But who it was that appeared, and of what kind, and in what manner, and to which part of us, they have left to be examined by those able to make themselves like the men to whom God appeared; for he was seen not by their bodily eyes but by their pure heart. For, according to our Jesus, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

choices.choice: ‘To the Piraeus’ quotes the opening of Plato’s Republic (1.327a), where Socrates goes down to pray to ‘the goddess’; Plato’s goddess there is the Thracian Bendis, but Origen names Artemis, and the translation follows Origen. ‘A cock to Asclepius’ is Socrates’ last request (Phaedo 118a). Both classical citations are certain. ‘Artemis as a goddess’ renders ὡς θεῷ (the Greek uses the common-gender θεός of a pagan deity; lowercase). εἰς τιμήν φησιν ἐκείνου: φησιν is singular (‘so he says’ / ‘so it is said’), and ἐκείνου most likely means the god whom the image is said to honour; rendered ‘in honour, so they say, of that being’. 1 Corinthians 1:27–28 is quoted in fragments and in an order different from Paul’s (Paul’s ‘weak things’ shame ‘the strong’); kept as Origen gives it. ἀγενῆ rendered ‘base things’. The ‘appeared’ passages: the triad Abraham, Isaac, Jacob with ὤφθη fits Exodus 6:3, and the individual appearances are Genesis 12:7, 26:24 and 35:9; Origen says ‘for example’, so these are representative, not a single quotation. πρῶτον is taken as ‘were the first (to know)’, marking their priority over Plato; it could also mean ‘first of all’. (ἑαυτὸν) is Koetschau’s supplement. Review: ὡς θεοῦ ἐμφανίζοντος gives the writers’ ground (‘since God shows himself’), not an unreal comparison, so ‘as though’ was dropped. ὀφθεὶς αὐτῶν ... τῇ καθαρᾷ καρδίᾳ: αὐτῶν is genitive with the eyes and heart (‘their bodily eyes’, ‘their pure heart’), not an agent. φησιν has no named subject, so ‘so it is said’; it may point to a pagan defence of images, possibly Celsus’s own.
'as though God showed himself' -> 'since God shows himself' (ὡς + genitive absolute is causal, not counterfactual)
'seen by them not with the eyes of the body but with the pure heart' -> 'seen not by their bodily eyes but by their pure heart' (αὐτῶν is possessive)
'which of the things within us' -> 'which part of us' (calque removed)
'so they say' -> 'so it is said' (φησιν, singular, no subject named)
'is "by no means" to be "spoken"' -> 'can "by no means" be "spoken"' (ῥητόν)
checked Republic 1.327a, Phaedo 118a, Romans 1:19-25, 1 Corinthians 1:27-29, Genesis 12:7, 26:24, 35:9, Exodus 6:3, Matthew 5:8; all correct
